summary: Defines procedures for dynamically signaled hierarchical label switched paths in MPLS and GMPLS networks, where one LSP is used as a link carrying other traffic. It adds mechanisms to establish such LSPs and uses them as traffic engineering links. It updates RFC 3477 and RFC 4206.

eli5.summary: Think of a big highway tunnel that other roads use as one stretch of road. This explains how routers set up that tunnel on demand.

questions: what is a forwarding adjacency in gmpls
what does the lsp tunnel interface id object do
subtitle: Lets the two ends of an MPLS or GMPLS tunnel agree during setup how it will be used as a link.

tldr.problem: An LSP used as a link in another network had to be configured by hand at both ends, and the old numbered signaling method was inefficient and gave the egress no hint of the intended use.
tldr.mechanism: The LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object gets new Class Types with an Actions flags field and optional TLVs that say how the LSP is used, which IGP instance advertises it, and which link bundle it joins.
tldr.outcome: Both ends can set up and advertise the new link from signaling alone, and the older RFC 4206 method for numbered forwarding adjacencies is deprecated.

today: RFC 6107 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3477 and RFC 4206, and it deprecates the RFC 4206 technique for signaling numbered TE links. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Problem and Goals
sections.content:
Traffic engineering (TE) links in an MPLS or GMPLS network may be built from Label Switched Paths (LSPs). Such LSPs are called hierarchical LSPs (H-LSPs). An LSP in one network may serve as a TE link in another, for example when an optical server network supplies links to a packet client network.

Many parallel TE links can be grouped and advertised as a single link bundle. Deployment showed problems in how the two LSP endpoints coordinate the use of the LSP and the identifiers of its endpoints. This document defines how the ends exchange whether the LSP is ordinary or hierarchical, which IGP instances should advertise it, how clients use it, whether it joins a bundle, and how the link ends are identified.
sections.eli5: When two towns build a tunnel that other roads will use, both towns need to agree what the tunnel is for. Now they can tell each other while building it.

sections.title: Existing Mechanisms and Their Gaps
sections.content:
A Forwarding Adjacency (FA) is a link created from an LSP and advertised in the same routing instance that advertises the links the LSP crosses. RFC 3477 signals unnumbered FAs using an LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object that carries each end's Router ID and interface ID. It has no support for IPv6 or numbered identifiers.

RFC 4206 creates numbered IPv4 FAs differently: the ingress uses one address of a /31 pair, and the egress infers the other. The egress learns it must advertise a reverse link only by watching the ingress advertisement and matching it against its LSPs. The RFC calls this inefficient and poorly scaling.

There was also no way to say an LSP is a private link, a link for a different IGP instance, or a bundle component. An informal survey in the CCAMP working group found no significant deployments of the numbered-FA technique, so this document deprecates it.
sections.eli5: The old way made one end guess what the other wanted by watching announcements. That was slow, so the new way just tells it directly.

sections.title: The Extended Interface ID Object
sections.content:
The LSP_TUNNEL_INTERFACE_ID object (C-NUM 193) gains three Class Types: C-Type 4 for unnumbered links, C-Type 2 for IPv4 numbered links and C-Type 3 for IPv6 numbered links. Each carries an interface identifier or address, an 8-bit Actions field, reserved bits and optional TLVs. C-Type 1 keeps working unchanged.

The Actions field has five flags, meaningful on a Path message. On a Resv message the field SHOULD echo the Path value and MUST be ignored on receipt.

  • P (Private): 1 means a private link that is not advertised in the IGP.
  • T (TE link): 1 means the LSP is not used as a TE link.
  • R (Routing adjacency): 1 means the link forms a routing adjacency.
  • B (Bundle): 1 means the LSP is part of a link bundle.
  • H (Hierarchy/stitching): 0 means a hierarchical LSP, 1 a stitching segment.

An LSP that is to form an FA carries Actions set to 0x00. In a Path message the object is the Forward Interface ID, and in a Resv message it is the Reverse Interface ID.
sections.eli5: The object is like a form with checkboxes: is this tunnel private, is it a road, does it connect neighbors, is it part of a bundle, and is it a tunnel or a stitched stretch.

sections.title: IGP Instance and Component Link TLVs
sections.content:
The object can carry TLVs, each with a 16-bit type and a 16-bit length, padded to a multiple of four octets. Four types are defined: 1 for the IGP Instance Identifier, 2 for the Unnumbered Component Link Identifier, 3 for the IPv4 Numbered Component Link Identifier and 4 for the IPv6 Numbered Component Link Identifier.

The IGP Instance Identifier is a 32-bit number that tells the egress which IGP instance should advertise the link. Assigning the numbers is a management task outside the document. The value 0xffffffff is reserved to mean the same instance that advertises the links the LSP traverses. If the TLV is absent, that same instance is used.

When the B-flag is set, the interface identifiers, flags and IGP TLV describe the bundle itself, and exactly one component link TLV MUST be present in both the Path and Resv objects to identify the component link.
sections.eli5: Extra notes on the form say which map the new road goes on, and which bundle of roads it belongs to.

sections.title: Advertising and Tearing Down the Link
sections.content:
The ingress and egress MUST advertise the LSP as agreed in the object. A TE link created from the LSP SHOULD inherit the LSP's TE properties, subject to policy. One LSP may serve several networks, so multiple objects may appear in the same message, each with a different IGP Instance Identifier. A message MUST NOT contain more than one object with C-Type 1.

If the link is advertised in the same IGP instance as the links it crosses, addresses MUST come from the same address space. The ingress TE Router ID is taken from the Tunnel Sender Address in the Sender Template object. On teardown through a PathTear, or a PathErr with the Path_State_Removed flag set, the ends SHOULD withdraw the advertisement.

New implementations are RECOMMENDED to place the object immediately after SENDER_TSPEC in a Path message and after FILTER_SPEC in a Resv message.
sections.eli5: Once both ends agree, they both announce the new road. When the tunnel closes, they take the announcement back.

sections.title: Errors and Compatibility
sections.content:
An egress that cannot accept the parameters SHOULD answer with a PathErr using the new error code 38, LSP Hierarchy Issue. Values 1 to 16 cover cases such as unsupported or policy-forbidden link advertisement, TE link creation, routing adjacency and bundle creation, unsupported hierarchy or stitching, unknown IGP instance, and invalid or missing component link identifiers. Where the error arises after setup, the PathErr SHOULD be sent with Path_State_Removed clear so the LSP stays up. An ingress that rejects a Resv SHOULD send a PathTear.

Because the object has class number 193, nodes that do not understand it forward it unchanged under RFC 2205, so transit nodes are unaffected. A back-level egress rejects Path messages with the new Class Types, which tells the ingress it is back-level. C-Type 1 still works with old and new nodes.
sections.eli5: If a town cannot or may not do what is asked, it replies with a numbered reason. Older towns just say they do not understand, and that is fine.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The extensions are not seen as an added security risk, and may arguably make RSVP messages harder to spoof. An ingress asking an egress to advertise an LSP as a TE link MUST be subject to policy checks at the egress, which MUST NOT accept the ingress's word unless configured with such a policy. The RFC refers to RFC 5920 for further security detail on MPLS-TE and GMPLS.
sections.eli5: The far end should not do whatever it is told without checking its own rules first.
